newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ yields close higher as political factors bite.
newsitem.headline: NZ yields close higher as political factors bite.

text.p: New Zealand yields closed sharply higher on Monday on a combination of U.S. weakness on Friday and local political factors.
Turnover was light in the afternoon after yields were marked up sharply in the morning but yields kept edging higher, signifying a bear market, dealers said.
A TV3 political opinion poll tonight may give the market further information to feed on after a TV1 poll published on Sunday gave the market mixed news.

Some dealers said that while the ruling National Party lost four points to 35 percent, the poll was not so negative because two of its potential allies, the Christian Coalition and radical free-market ACT, were up near the five percent threshold needed to win seats.
A general election is due on October 12.
Dealers said bidding in the 7/98s held the market in a bit but the long bonds lost 11 points versus three in Australia, suggesting political risk was the distinguishing factor.

"It's definitely political risk being priced in," said one dealer. "The poll confirmed a worsening trend for National being saved all-in-all by the Christians and ACT coming near to that threshold. But overall it is not a great trend. It doesn't bode well and it certainly doesn't make people feel comfortable."
December bank bill futures closed nine points down at 90.69 while the September contract was five off at 90.10.
Dealers said there was still quite an overhang of last week's Samurai issues to feed through in the two year bonds.

Peter McTeague of MCM TradeWatch said more of a political risk premium associated with the October 12 election needed to be reflected in the shape of the coupon curve. At 15 basis points, the coupon curve did not accurately reflect the possibility of a non-National Party coaltion gaining power.
Additionally, he said the long-end of the curve was running into resistance.
Unless the 10 years could break below the psychological 8.0 percent level, the bias would remain towards a steeper curve.
